subject: treasureChest
reasoning:
I'm planning out a stylized treasure chest model in TypeScript using the SDK, designing a wooden chest with a curved lid, iron bands, lock, handle, and gold coins/gems spilling out, positioned to stand at y=0 and face +Z.

I'm sticking to APIs I'm confident about: createBuilder, b.joint, b.part, b.stick, and b.root, building the body as a box and the lid as a half-cylinder rotated to form a curved top, with a hinge joint along the back edge for the lid. I'm also considering adding plain three.js meshes directly to the root joint for extra details like coins and gems, since objects attached to b.root ride along with it automatically.

Given the uncertainty around joints, I'll simplify by skipping bone hierarchies entirely and using a single "chest" joint since rigging isn't needed for this static model. Now I'm defining the geometry pieces: a brown wood box for the body, and a half-cylinder lid rotated so its axis runs along X instead of the default Y.

Working through the rotation math, I confirm the half-cylinder's flat bottom face sits directly on top of the box at the correct height and depth alignment, so the lid appears as a solid closed shape sitting flush on the body without any visible gaps or hidden faces.

Now I'm adding iron bands as dark gray thin half-cylinders wrapping over the lid near its ends, using an open-ended cylinder geometry with a slightly larger radius so they sit just outside the lid surface for a decorative strap effect.

I'm sketching the remaining hardware: vertical front straps, a gold lock plate with a dark keyhole detail, and side handles made from half-torus rings rotated to lie flush against the chest's ends.

Setting the ring in a ZY plane means it's flat against the end face, which isn't right — I need the handle to actually stick out from the face rather than lie flush against it, so I should rethink the orientation of the torus.

Actually, let me simplify and skip the handle rings entirely, using corner brackets instead to avoid the plane confusion. I'm now thinking about opening the chest lid for the coin pile — hinging it at the back top edge and rotating the lid geometry around that pivot axis to create an open-lid pose.

Still working out lid positioning math...

Since the open lid is a rotated half-cylinder, its underside becomes visible, which is fine. For the interior, I want a dark cavity look, so I'll add a thin dark plane just below the box's top surface to simulate the inside of the container.

For the contents, I'm planning a heap of gold coins using small low-poly cylinders scattered within the interior rectangle, favoring deterministic sine-based positioning over a random generator to avoid API uncertainty. I'll also scatter a few low-poly gem spheres in red and blue among the coins, with some stacked higher to form a small mound rising above the rim since the lid is open and there's room for height.

Now I'm shifting to the chest's body structure: feet as small dark boxes at the four corners, a body box roughly 0.5 units tall with its base around y=0.1 and top meeting the lid base at y=0.6, adjusting lid and band positions to match. I'm adding vertical straps on the front and back faces, plus a lid band made from a half-cylinder arc positioned at the same radius as the lid, translated into place at its base height.

I'm working out a shared helper transform to pivot and rotate the lid geometry so bands on the lid rotate consistently with it, making sure the pivot point for the arc lines up at y=0 so the lid opens correctly around its hinge.

The underside of the open lid will just show its flat half-disc shape, which is fine, and the chest's hollow interior reads correctly since the hinge sits at the back edge while the front rises up. For the coin pile, I'm working out a deterministic pseudo-random placement using sine-based hash functions, scattering around 36 flat cylindrical coins within the chest's opening and giving them a mound-like height profile so they pile higher toward the center and taper off near the edges.

Adding gem accents...

Now I'm placing the lock mechanism — a gold plate centered on the front face with a small dark keyhole cutout slightly protruding outward from it.

Still placing hardware...

I'll skip plank seam decoration to keep things simple, then set up the module with a single root joint since one bone is sufficient here. Writing the imports and color constants, then starting the builder code with helper functions for geometry placement.

Still writing builder logic...

Now working out the lid hinge mechanics, using a half-cylinder geometry rotated so its arc forms the curved lid shape, carefully tracking the axis transformations to make sure the pivot point and open-rotation math line up correctly.

Adding reinforcement bands around the lid, an interior panel to cover the body's top opening, a coin mound, and metal straps wrapped around the chest body at the front and back positions.

Now I'm detailing corner posts, a gold lock plate with a keyhole, small feet for the chest to stand on, and scattering a few loose coins and gems near the base for extra flair.

For the mound of coins itself, I'm randomizing coin positions in an elliptical footprint within the chest's interior, tilting each coin slightly for a natural scattered look, and varying their height based on distance from the pile's center so they stack higher toward the middle.

For the gems sitting on top of the mound, I'm placing them at specific x/z coordinates and approximating their resting height using the same surface-height formula as the coins, just offset slightly upward so they appear nestled into the pile rather than floating above it.

The lid is hinged at the back and opens upward, so I confirm it won't intersect the chest's contents even at the pile's highest point — everything checks out, so I'll finalize the geometry and return the built chest root.
